passages.title: Compasses in the Sky
passages.passage: Few sights in nature rival thousands of geese lifting off a marsh at dawn, yet the mechanics of how they find their way are (1)____ to be fully understood. What is certain is that no single sense accounts for the feat. Birds appear to draw (2)____ a whole toolkit: the setting sun, the rotating stars, the smell of the coast and, most remarkably, the Earth's magnetic field, which they seem to perceive through specialised proteins in the eye. (3)____ sooner had researchers demonstrated this magnetic sense in the laboratory than a new puzzle arose, for a compass tells a traveller which way is north but not where it currently is. Somehow the birds manage (4)____ only to hold a heading but also to correct for being blown hundreds of kilometres off course. Young birds on their first journey seem to inherit a rough programme, an instruction to fly in a given direction for a given number of weeks, (5)____ older birds refine this with a memory of landmarks built up over previous seasons. This would explain why juveniles displaced by storms tend to end (6)____ in the wrong place while adults usually recover. The costs are severe: a small warbler may lose nearly half its body weight crossing the Sahara, and every year countless birds fail to complete the trip. (7)____ the risks, the strategy persists because the rewards, chiefly the brief but enormous abundance of insects in the northern summer, outweigh them. Nowadays, however, timing that evolution fine-tuned over millennia is being thrown (8)____ of step with a warming climate. Insects are emerging earlier, and birds (9)____ arrive on the old schedule find the feast already over. Whether they can adjust quickly enough is a question (10)____ which the answer, for many species, will decide their survival.

questions.explanation: Be yet to (or be still to) means something has not happened up to now: the mechanics are yet to be fully understood. Far would need from, not to be, and not cannot stand alone before to be here.

To draw on (or draw upon) resources means to make use of them, which is what the birds do with their toolkit of senses. Draw from is used for taking something out of a source, and draw in means attract.
The inverted structure No sooner had … than … means one event followed immediately after another. Hardly or scarcely would need when, not than, and neither combines with sooner.
The correlative pair not only … but also links the two infinitives to hold and to correct. Never or no would break the pairing with but also, and just cannot be followed by only.

The sentence contrasts what young birds do with what older birds do, so a contrast linker such as while or whereas fits; a plain and or but is also acceptable. Because or so would wrongly make one behaviour the cause or result of the other.

The phrasal verb end up (somewhere) means finish a journey in that place, often unintentionally. End in describes the outcome of an event, not a location, and end at is not idiomatic with a wrong place.

A concessive word is needed before the noun phrase the risks: Despite (or Notwithstanding, or Whatever) the risks, the strategy persists. Although is a conjunction and would need a clause with a verb after it, and For on its own does not work here: the idiom is For all the risks, with all.

To be out of step with something is to no longer match it, and thrown out of step is the natural collocation. Off would need a different noun (thrown off course), and away does not combine with of step.
A defining relative pronoun is needed to identify which birds: birds that (or which) arrive on the old schedule. Who is normally reserved for people, and whose would need a following noun.
The formal relative structure a question to which the answer … keeps the preposition in front of which: the answer to a question. Of or for do not collocate with answer in this sense.

passages.title: Stone Statements
passages.passage: To the modern visitor a castle is a romantic ruin, but to the people who built one it was (1)____ more than a fortress: it was a statement. The earliest examples in Britain were little more than earth mounds topped with wooden towers, thrown (2)____ in weeks by conquerors who needed to hold territory before the local population could organise resistance. Only later, once the land was secure, (3)____ stone replace timber, and with stone came a new scale of ambition. A great keep might take twenty years to complete and consume the income of an entire region, which is (4)____ so few lords could afford one. The design was anything but haphazard. Walls were angled so that attackers approaching the gate would be exposed to arrows from two sides at (5)____; staircases spiralled clockwise so that a defender retreating upwards could swing his sword freely while an attacker below could not. Even the latrines, which emptied into the moat, played a part (6)____ discouraging anyone from swimming across. Yet for all its military ingenuity, a castle was rarely taken by assault. Far more often the besiegers simply waited, cutting (7)____ supplies until hunger did the work that catapults could not. Had gunpowder never reached Europe, the castle might have survived for centuries; (8)____ it was, the cannon made high walls a liability rather than a strength within a few generations. By the sixteenth century the nobility had abandoned the keep for the comfortable country house, and the fortresses they left behind were quarried for their stone. What remains today is, in most cases, (9)____ a fraction of the original, and it takes a considerable act of imagination to picture the noise, smoke and crowding of a castle in (10)____ prime.

questions.explanation: Far more than (or much more than) intensifies the comparison: the castle was not merely a fortress. Very cannot modify a comparative, and even would suggest an unexpected addition rather than an intensified one.
To throw up a structure is to build it hastily, exactly what conquerors in a hurry did. Throw out means discard, and throw down means hurl to the ground; neither describes rapid building.

A sentence beginning with restrictive Only later triggers inversion, so the auxiliary did comes before the subject stone: only later did stone replace timber. Was would need a passive participle, and no inversion at all would be ungrammatical after Only later.

Which is why introduces the consequence of the enormous cost: few lords could afford a keep. Because would reverse the direction of cause and effect, and how would describe a method rather than a reason.
At once here means at the same time: arrows came from two sides simultaneously. At last would mean finally, and at all only works in negative or question contexts.
The collocation is play a part in doing something, so in is followed by the -ing form discouraging. Of and for do not combine with play a part.

To cut off supplies is to prevent them from reaching their destination, which is what a besieging army did. Cut down means reduce, and cut out means remove or stop entirely, neither of which describes a blockade.

The idiom as it was means in reality, as things actually turned out, and it answers the preceding unreal conditional. How it was or so it was do not carry this contrast between the imagined and the real.

A limiting adverb such as only (or just, merely, formal but) stresses how little survives: only a fraction of the original. Even would imply surprise that so much remains, the opposite of the intended sense.
The idiom in its prime means at the height of its strength; the possessive refers back to a castle. It's is a contraction of it is, and the prime is not idiomatic with a subject.

passages.title: Seeing Red, Feeling Blue
passages.passage: Ask a group of people to name a calming colour and most (1)____ them will say blue; ask for an alarming one and red will win by a wide margin. Such agreement is striking, and it has led many to conclude that colour acts on the mind directly, (2)____ of culture or experience. The evidence, however, is far from straightforward. It is true that red has been shown to raise the pulse slightly and that athletes wearing it win marginally more often, an effect (3)____ to the association between red and dominance in many species. Yet the same colour signals luck in one country and danger in another, and a bride dressed in white would be a cause for grief in cultures where white is the colour of mourning. What seems innate, in other words, may be (4)____ more than a habit learnt so early that we no longer notice having learnt it. Marketing departments have not waited for the argument to be settled. Fast-food chains favour warm colours on the (5)____ that they stimulate appetite and encourage customers to eat quickly and leave; banks lean towards navy and grey, shades that are supposed to suggest stability, (6)____ the balance sheet actually says. Whether these choices work is another matter: a company (7)____ logo is the wrong shade of orange will not go bankrupt on that account. The most robust finding is perhaps the least dramatic. Colour affects us, but only in context, only briefly, and only at the margins. Anyone who claims that painting a classroom green will make children behave has, (8)____ all likelihood, mistaken a fashion for a law of nature, and it is worth remembering that such claims (9)____ been made, and quietly abandoned, for well (10)____ a century.

questions.explanation: Before a pronoun, a quantifier needs of: most of them. Most them is ungrammatical, and most people would not need of but here the word after the blank is them.

Regardless of (or irrespective of, independently of) means without being affected by, which fits the claim that colour works on everyone the same way. Despite and instead cannot be followed by of with this meaning.
An effect attributed to a cause (or attributable, due, owing, linked, related to) says where the effect comes from. Caused is impossible because it would need by, not to.
Little more than (or nothing more than, no more than) plays down the supposed instinct as merely a habit. Much more than would say the opposite, and far would also intensify rather than minimise.

On the grounds that (or on the assumption, theory, basis, premise, understanding, belief that) gives the reason for a decision. Reason would need for the reason that, not on the, and ground in the singular is not the idiom.

Whatever the balance sheet actually says means the colours are meant to suggest stability no matter what the real figures show. Despite is a preposition and cannot be followed directly by a clause, and however would need an adjective or adverb after it.
The possessive relative whose links the company to its logo: a company whose logo is the wrong shade. Which or that would leave logo without a determiner, and its cannot introduce a relative clause.
The fixed phrase is in all likelihood, meaning very probably. With or by are not used with likelihood in this idiom.

The time phrase for well over a century reaches up to the present, so the present perfect passive is needed: such claims have been made. Had would place the claims before some other past point, and were would need a finished period.

Well over a century means considerably more than a hundred years; well above is a rarer but defensible alternative. Well more than is not idiomatic, and beyond does not combine with well before a period of time in this way.

passages.title: Harvest from the Sand
passages.passage: Growing food where rain falls only a few times a year sounds futile, yet farmers have done precisely that for thousands of years, and their methods are attracting fresh attention as the climate warms. The oldest trick is simply to (1)____ the most of what little water there is. In the Negev, ancient farmers channelled the run-off from bare hillsides into small walled fields, (2)____ a single storm could deliver the equivalent of a season's rain. Modern versions, from drip irrigation to buried clay pots that release moisture slowly, (3)____ on the same principle: deliver water to the root and nowhere else. Choice of crop matters just as much. Date palms and millet can (4)____ levels of heat and salt that would kill wheat within days, and breeders are now combing wild relatives of common crops for drought-tolerance genes. Perhaps the most ambitious projects, however, are those that set (5)____ to reverse the desert's advance altogether. Along the Sahara's edge, rows of trees are being planted to hold back the dunes and shade the soil, keeping evaporation (6)____ a minimum and slowly restoring the organic matter that overgrazing stripped away. Critics note that such schemes have a poor record; too many have been (7)____ with great fanfare and then quietly forgotten once the funding dried up. There is also the question of who owns the water. Pumping fossil aquifers to grow fodder for export may pay in the (8)____ term, but the water took ten thousand years to accumulate and will not be replaced. (9)____ desert farming can feed the growing populations of the world's dry regions depends less on technology than on whether governments will value water as the scarce resource it is. Without that shift, even the cleverest irrigation will do little more than put (10)____ the inevitable.

questions.q: Blank (1): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: The idiom is make the most of something, meaning use it as fully as possible. Take and get combine with the most only as quantities, and do the most is not a set phrase.

questions.q: Blank (2): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: Whereby means by means of which: the fields were the arrangement through which one storm delivered a season's rain. Whereas contrasts, whereupon means immediately after which, and wherein would refer to a place or document, not a method.

questions.q: Blank (3): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: An idea or method rests on a principle, meaning it is based on it. Stand on principle is a different idiom (refuse to compromise), and lie on or sit on describe physical position.

questions.q: Blank (4): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: A plant tolerates heat and salt when it can survive them. Accept, allow and permit all involve agreeing to something, which a crop cannot do; they are near misses because tolerate can also mean put up with in human contexts.

questions.q: Blank (5): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: Set out to do something means begin with that as your aim. Set about must be followed by an -ing form, set off means depart on a journey, and set up means establish.

questions.q: Blank (6): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: The collocation is keep something to a minimum, meaning make it as small as possible. At a minimum means at the very least, a different idea, and in or on do not combine with minimum.

questions.q: Blank (7): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: A scheme or campaign is launched, and launched with great fanfare is the standard collocation. Films and products are released, statements are issued, and goods or speeches are delivered.

questions.q: Blank (8): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is in the short term, contrasting with the long term. Brief, small and quick share the idea of limited size or time but do not collocate with term.

questions.q: Blank (9): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: A clause acting as the subject of depends must begin with Whether. If cannot introduce a subject clause, and Unless or Although would leave the main verb depends without a subject.

questions.q: Blank (10): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: To put off something is to postpone it, so an irrigation system can only put off the inevitable. Put away means store, put down means place or suppress, and put out means extinguish or publish.
